content: Fetal fibronectin (FFN) is an extracellular matrix glycoprotein located at the maternal-fetal interface, specifically between the chorion and decidua of the amniotic membranes. Under normal physiological conditions, FFN is present in cervicovaginal secretions at very low concentrations. However, levels of FFN equal to or exceeding 50 ng/mL, particularly after 22 weeks of gestation, have been associated with an increased risk of spontaneous preterm birth. FFN is considered one of the most reliable biomarkers for predicting preterm birth across various populations and can assist in identifying women at significant risk for this condition. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of clinical management strategies informed by FFN testing results in preventing preterm birth. This review is an update of a previous analysis first published in 2008. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of September 7, 2018. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared outcomes in pregnant women whose management was guided by FFN test results versus those whose management was not influenced by such knowledge. Studies that exclusively included women with either positive or negative FFN results were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified the accuracy of the findings. The quality of the evidence was appraised using the GRADE methodology. A total of 16 trials were identified, of which six met the inclusion criteria. These six trials involved 546 women with singleton pregnancies and symptoms of threatened preterm labor between 23 weeks and 34 weeks and 6 days of gestation. Among these participants, 277 women were randomized to a group where FFN test results were known, while 269 women were assigned to a group where FFN results were not disclosed. No trials were identified that included asymptomatic women or those with multiple gestations. The risk of bias across the included studies was variable. For key outcomes, such as preterm birth before 37, 34, and 32 weeks of gestation, as well as maternal hospitalization, the quality of evidence was generally low due to imprecise effect estimates. Management strategies based on FFN test results may reduce the incidence of preterm birth before 37 weeks, with 20.7% of women in the FFN-informed group delivering preterm compared to 29.2% in the control group (risk ratio [RR] 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.52 to 1.01; 5 trials; 434 women; low-quality evidence). However, FFN-informed management appears to have little or no effect on preterm birth before 34 weeks (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.18; 4 trials; 357 women; low-quality evidence) or maternal hospitalization (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.43; 5 trials; 441 women; low-quality evidence). The evidence regarding preterm birth before 32 weeks was deemed very uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (average RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.16 to 3.96; 4 trials; 357 women). For other outcomes, such as preterm birth before 28 weeks, gestational age at delivery, birthweight under 2500 grams, perinatal death, use of tocolytics, administration of corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, time to clinical evaluation, respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, and NICU length of stay, the knowledge of FFN results appeared to have little or no impact. In conclusion, the findings of this review suggest that management strategies informed by FFN test results may reduce the risk of preterm birth before 37 weeks. However, the confidence in this finding is limited due to the low quality of the evidence. The effects of FFN-informed management on other clinically significant outcomes remain uncertain, primarily due to concerns regarding study design, inconsistency, and imprecision in the effect estimates. No trials were identified that included asymptomatic women or those with multiple gestations. Future research should focus on specific populations, such as women with singleton pregnancies and symptoms of preterm labor, and should evaluate both maternal and perinatal outcomes. Additionally, cost-effectiveness analyses are warranted to better understand the utility of FFN testing in clinical practice.
